slides.title: Chapter 1: Introduction
slides.say: This chapter answers one question: what is Bitcoin, and why does every part of it exist? Point at the coin on circuit traces and ask what students already believe Bitcoin is. Common first answers are an app or a company; the better answer is a ledger that many computers keep together.
slides.takeaway: What Bitcoin is, what it is made of, and why every part of it exists

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Six parts follow the order a first payment needs them. Point at the three counters on the right: slides, true stories and runnable examples. Ask which part students feel least sure about. Every example has a twin in the Chapter Examples tab of the course page, so they can rerun it at home.
slides.takeaway: Six parts, fifteen examples, nine true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Read the six questions aloud and promise to answer them in the summary. Ask who can already answer the first. A common answer lists inventors; the better one is that Bitcoin combined four earlier parts, which part 2 shows.
slides.takeaway: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

slides.title: One chapter, six branches
slides.say: This map is the skeleton of the lecture: one root and six branches. Point at the branch we are about to enter each time we move on. Ask which branch looks hardest. Remind students that the course page has the same map to click through.
slides.takeaway: Six branches; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Origins
slides.say: The first part has three beats: the first block, the first payment and the forty years before. Read each comparison aloud. Ask what a time capsule has in common with a block. A common slip is to treat the headline as decoration; it is a dated proof.
slides.takeaway: Bitcoin combines old parts, like a recipe of familiar ingredients.

slides.title: Origins: key concepts
slides.say: Two cards open the chapter: what the introduction promises and how the history fits. Read each card twice, once for the meaning and once for the comparison. Ask a student to retell the family-tree comparison. The usual mistake is to learn history as dates instead of as parts that Bitcoin reuses.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A newspaper headline carved into block zero
slides.say: Tell this one as a story. Point at the hex dump and at the source link; anyone can open this block today. Ask why a newspaper headline proves a date. A common mistake is to read it as a message to the public; it is a timestamp for the future.
slides.takeaway: Recorded: 3 January 2009

slides.title: The headline inside block zero
slides.say: The code cuts the first block's script into eight bytes of pushes and the text. Point at the result [8, 69] and at the headline in the box beside it. Ask where 77 comes from: eight plus sixty-nine. Students often forget that bytes become text only after decode.
slides.takeaway: The first block carries its own date: a newspaper headline

slides.title: The first person ever paid in bitcoin
slides.say: Two people, one shared ledger, no bank. Point at the photograph of Hal Finney and at block 170 in the link. Ask why the first payment went to a cryptographer. A common mistake is to call Finney the first miner; he ran the software and received the coins.
slides.takeaway: Satoshi Nakamoto, and the cryptographer who ran the code

slides.title: Forty years of failed digital money
slides.say: Four names, four parts, forty years. Point at the photograph of David Chaum and ask which part each person built. A common mistake is to say Bitcoin invented digital cash; the white paper cites these systems and adds proof of work.
slides.takeaway: Every part existed before Bitcoin combined them

slides.title: Four near misses, one combination
slides.say: Read the timeline from 1982 to 2009 and stop at each name. Ask what the four near misses had in common. None could agree on one history without a leader. Students often mix up the dates, so point at 1982, 1997, 1998 and 2008.
slides.takeaway: The pieces were old; the combination was new

slides.title: Money and price
slides.say: Money is a ledger of who owns what, and Bitcoin keeps that ledger in public. Read the three beats: what money was, units and supply, price and exchange. Ask what a scoreboard and a bank balance have in common. Both work only because everyone trusts the record.
slides.takeaway: Money is a ledger of who owns what; Bitcoin keeps that ledger in public.

slides.title: Money and price: key concepts
slides.say: Four cards: the floating exchange rate, how a fair daily price is found, the currency exchange and the Bitcoin ATM. Ask why the tomato stall is a good comparison for price. Students often think someone sets the price; the next slides show that trades do.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The island where money never moved
slides.say: On Yap the stones stayed where they were and only the memory of ownership moved. Point at the photograph and ask what the ledger was. The shared memory of the village. A common mistake is to focus on the size of the stones instead of the record.

read.label: Furness: The Island of Stone Money (book)

slides.takeaway: Documented in 1903; the free ebook edition came in 2024

slides.title: Five thousand years to digital cash
slides.say: Walk the timeline from grain ledgers to 15 August 1971. Point at the coin photograph and the link to the money museum. Ask who keeps the ledger in each age. The common slip is to say fiat money has no ledger; bank balances are one.
slides.takeaway: From grain ledgers to pure fiat money, 3000 BCE to 1971

slides.title: Traditional, digital, crypto: side by side
slides.say: This is the chapter's one table. Read the first column down, then compare the three money kinds across each row. Ask who keeps the ledger in cash, and the answer is nobody; possession is the record. Students often miss that Bitcoin settles in about an hour, not instantly.
slides.takeaway: Same uses, different ledgers: that difference is this course

slides.title: The internet got payments - and new gatekeepers
slides.say: Tell the PayPal story as a lesson in gatekeepers. Point at the logo and at the names Levchin, Thiel and Musk. Ask what the internet still lacked after 2002, and the answer is cash that needs no company between payer and payee. A common mistake is to think online payment equals digital cash.
slides.takeaway: The dot-com boom digitised paying, not cash

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.say: A war stopped ordinary payments, and an open network kept working. Point at the photograph of Mykhailo Fedorov and the 54.7 million dollars. Ask what the donors needed to send help, and the answer is only an address. Check the CNBC source together; do not repeat figures from memory.
slides.takeaway: Ukraine, February 2022: a state turns to an open payment network

slides.title: When the money in your hand stops working
slides.say: Five documented cases, each with its own link: Kenya, Cyprus, Greece, Venezuela and Ukraine. Point at one photograph per case. Ask which case is about trust in banks and which about access. A common mistake is to treat these as hypotheticals; every one is sourced.
slides.takeaway: Crisis or war, banked or not: the need is documented

slides.title: A bitcoin counted in satoshis
slides.say: A bitcoin is counted in whole satoshis, a hundred million to the coin. Point at the result [100000000, 100000, 1] and at the exact conversion of 0.001. Ask why exact whole numbers matter for money. Floating-point decimals would drift; students often type 0.001 as a float.
slides.takeaway: Money here is counting, and the units are exact

slides.title: The subsidy at five block heights
slides.say: The subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks. Point at the five heights and at the result 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, 3.125. Ask what the next value is, and the answer is half of 3.125. Students often think halving happens by date; it happens by block height.
slides.takeaway: Every halving cuts new issuance in half

slides.title: The 21 million cap is a sum
slides.say: The cap is arithmetic, not a promise. Point at the one-line sum over 33 eras and at the result, just under 21 million. Ask why it is not exactly 21 million. Each era drops fractions below one satoshi, so the total ends at 20,999,999.9769.
slides.takeaway: Scarcity is arithmetic that every node can re-run

slides.title: A central bank's jobs, done by rules
slides.say: A central bank decides how much money exists and a clearing house settles payments; Bitcoin does both by rule. Point at the three rows. Ask which institution each row replaces. Deflationary is a tendency of a fixed supply, not a promise of rising prices.
slides.takeaway: Rules every node checks replace three institutions' jobs

slides.title: Where a price comes from
slides.say: A price is where a buyer and a seller meet. Point at the gap between the highest bid and the lowest ask in the toy book. Ask what happens when a buyer raises the bid to the ask, and the answer is a trade, and that trade becomes the last price. The numbers are illustrative.
slides.takeaway: A price is the last place a buyer and a seller agreed

slides.title: No one sets the price: trades do
slides.say: A price is a ratio, and a day's figure is a weighted average. Point at the three trades and the result 62,764.71. Ask why a plain average would mislead. The big trade of one bitcoin should count more than the small one of 0.2.
slides.takeaway: Everyone who trades sets the price a little

slides.title: Two pizzas for ten thousand bitcoin
slides.say: The first purchase made a price exist. Point at the plaque photograph and the Guinness link. Ask what Hanyecz needed to know before he could set a price, and the answer is nothing yet existed to compare with. A common mistake is to say the pizzas were worth a lot; the point is the first price.
slides.takeaway: 22 May 2010: the day a price began to exist

slides.title: The Pizza Day coins, repriced
slides.say: The same ten thousand coins at six moments, drawn on a log axis. Point at the first bar, 41 dollars, and the last. Ask why a log axis is used. The values span seven orders of magnitude; on a plain axis the early bars would vanish.
slides.takeaway: From 41 dollars to 854 million: price discovery never stopped

slides.title: The network
slides.say: No bank sits in the middle: shared rules and shared work do its job. Read the three beats. Ask what neighbours who all keep a land register have in common with nodes, and the answer is each can check the others. A common mistake is to think a node is a server owned by Bitcoin.
slides.takeaway: No bank sits in the middle: shared rules and shared work do its job.

slides.title: A bank in the middle against peers
slides.say: Compare the bank in the middle with peers. Point at the single ledger-keeper on the left and at the ring of nodes on the right. Ask what happens if one node disappears, and the answer is nothing; the network still agrees. Decentralisation here is an architecture, not a slogan.
slides.takeaway: Remove any one node and the network still agrees

slides.title: The network: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.say: Three cards: proof of work, consensus and the double-spend. Read the jigsaw, the neighbours and the photocopied banknote. Ask why a hard puzzle that is easy to check is useful. Students often think proof of work solves something useful; its value is the cost.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Hard to find, easy to check
slides.say: A toy proof of work with hexadecimal zeros. Point at the result [9, 223, 1208, 57247]: each extra zero costs about sixteen times more guesses. Ask how many guesses checking needs, and the answer is one hash. Students often expect the search to be exactly sixteen times longer; it is an average.
slides.takeaway: Finding takes thousands of guesses; checking takes one hash

slides.title: Mining pays for honesty
slides.say: Mining pays for honesty. Follow the arrows from transactions waiting in the mempool to miners, a block about every ten minutes, and the reward. Ask why cheating costs more than it could win. Honest blocks pay in bitcoin; a rewrite spends energy for nothing.
slides.takeaway: Security is bought with energy and paid in bitcoin

slides.title: Keeping blocks ten minutes apart
slides.say: Difficulty adjustment keeps blocks near ten minutes whatever the total computing power. Point at the two cases: blocks too fast, target gets harder; too slow, easier. Ask why it needs 2016 blocks of evidence. One block is luck; two weeks of blocks are a measurement.
slides.takeaway: The network turns its own difficulty dial to hold the pace

slides.title: Why digital money had to wait
slides.say: A digital coin is a file, and files copy perfectly. Walk the three steps down the left, then the picture on the right where one coin reaches two shops. Ask what stopped this before Bitcoin, and the answer is a trusted central ledger. The mistake is to think encryption alone prevents copying.
slides.takeaway: A file can be copied; a coin must not be

slides.title: The double-spend, solved in public
slides.say: The double-spend is solved in public. Follow the numbered steps: every node hears both payments, they agree on one order, the first enters the block and the second is refused. Ask who plays referee. Nobody; the shared order does it.
slides.takeaway: Agreement on order is what removes the referee

slides.title: A double spend is refused
slides.say: One shared ledger, one rule. Point at the second pay call and at the result {'c1': 'bob'}: Carol never receives the coin. Ask what would happen without the rule, and the answer is both shops would see valid money. Students often expect an error message; the refusal is silent in this toy.
slides.takeaway: The second spend of a coin is refused everywhere

slides.title: A chain that notices tampering
slides.say: Each block hashes its text with the block before. Point at the change to block two and at the result 1. Ask which blocks are no longer trusted, and the answer is block two and everything after it. Students often think only the changed block fails.
slides.takeaway: Change one old block and every later link fails

slides.title: A chain of dated blocks
slides.say: A block holds a time and transactions, and carries the fingerprint of the block before. Point at the arrows that run backwards. Ask what happens when an old block is edited, and the answer is its fingerprint changes and every later link fails. A timestamp orders blocks; it does not make them true.
slides.takeaway: Edit one old block and every later link breaks

slides.title: The network: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.say: Two cards: confirmation and transaction fee. Read the cement comparison and the tip for the courier. Ask why a payment is not final the moment it is seen, and the answer is a later block could still replace it. Common mistake: confusing the fee with the amount paid to the receiver.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Confirmations pile up like layers
slides.say: Each block built on top adds another confirmation. Point at the staircase and at six confirmations, about an hour. Ask whether a payment is ever one hundred percent final, and the answer is it is only more and more costly to reverse. Irreversible here means practically, not magically.
slides.takeaway: Irreversible means ever costlier to reverse

slides.title: What the outputs leave over is the fee
slides.say: A transaction has no fee field. Point at the two outputs, 20,000 and 75,000, and at the result 5,000. Ask where a miner finds the fee, and the answer is it is whatever the outputs leave over. A forgotten change output turns into an expensive gift.
slides.takeaway: The fee is the part of the coin nobody was given

slides.title: Wallets and keys
slides.say: A wallet holds keys, not coins, like a ring of keys to many safes. Read the three beats. Ask what a pocket, a safe and a cloakroom ticket say about risk. Students often picture coins sitting inside the app; the coins live on the chain.
slides.takeaway: A wallet holds keys, not coins, like a ring of keys to many safes.

slides.title: The wallet branch, mapped
slides.say: Four questions place any wallet: platform, node type, key control and backup. Point at the four branches. Ask a student to place the phone app they use. Students often mix up node type and key control; they are independent choices.
slides.takeaway: Four questions place any wallet on this map

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (1 of 4)
slides.say: Three cards: getting started, choosing a wallet and the types of wallet, plus the desktop wallet. Read the bag, pocket and bicycle comparisons. Ask what makes one kind riskier. Who holds the keys and where the device runs.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (2 of 4)
slides.say: Four more kinds: mobile, web, hardware signing device and third-party API client. Ask which one is the cloakroom. The web wallet. A common mistake is to think a hardware wallet stores coins; it keeps keys and signs.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Five kinds of wallet compared
slides.say: Five kinds of wallet side by side. Read across a row: where the keys live, the main risk, the everyday comparison. Ask which row suits a small daily amount and which a large savings. A common mistake is to think a hardware wallet holds coins.
slides.takeaway: The kind of wallet decides who can lose or lock the keys

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (3 of 4)
slides.say: Full node, lightweight client, the comparison between them and who controls the keys. Ask who rereads every page of the ledger. The full node. Point at the last card: whoever holds the keys controls the coins.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Full node or lightweight client?
slides.say: A full node checks every rule itself; a lightweight client trusts the nodes it asks. Point at the trust row. Ask what you give up for convenience, and the answer is independence and some privacy. Students often think a lightweight wallet has no keys; it keeps them.
slides.takeaway: Checking for yourself costs storage; asking others costs trust

slides.title: Your key is your deed
slides.say: With a house the key opens and the registry proves; in Bitcoin the key does both. Point at the two columns and at the word deed. Ask what proof of ownership exists beyond the key, and the answer is none. A signature proves you hold the key while the key stays secret.
slides.takeaway: Prove you hold the key; never reveal it

slides.title: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins
slides.say: Custody is the first security decision. Compare full control with third-party control and point at the four device icons. Ask who can freeze coins in each column, and the answer is only the service in the right one. Students underestimate that backup becomes their own job.
slides.takeaway: Custody is the first security decision you make

slides.title: The exchange that lost everyone's coins
slides.say: Tell the Mt. Gox story with the date. Point at the logo and at the Tokyo District Court link. Ask where the keys were, and the answer is in the exchange's hands, not the customers'. A common mistake is to say the bitcoin were hacked on the blockchain; the loss was custody.
slides.takeaway: Tokyo, February 2014: balances on a website, keys elsewhere

slides.title: Where a wallet gets attacked
slides.say: Two common attacks: phishing asks you for the secret, malware steals it or changes the address you paste. Point at the three defences. Ask why no honest wallet ever asks for the recovery code in a web form. Anyone who has it owns the coins.
slides.takeaway: No honest wallet asks for the recovery code in a web form

slides.title: Wallets and keys: key concepts (4 of 4)
slides.say: Two cards: the noncustodial wallet and the recovery code. Read the home safe and the master key in the locker. Ask what twelve words can rebuild, and the answer is every key of the wallet. A common mistake is to photograph the words and store them online.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A recovery phrase becomes a seed
slides.say: A recovery phrase is stretched into a seed. Point at the three seeds for 1, 10 and 2048 rounds. Ask why slow is good here, and the answer is every guess of an attacker costs 2048 rounds. Students often think the seed is the phrase itself; it is derived from it.
slides.takeaway: Slow on purpose: every guess costs the full 2048 rounds

slides.title: A first payment
slides.say: From an empty wallet to a first payment, like a first driving lesson. Read the three beats. Ask what the first thing to do is, and the answer is write down the recovery code. A common slip is to buy bitcoin before the wallet is backed up.
slides.takeaway: From an empty wallet to a first payment, like a first driving lesson.

slides.title: A first payment: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.say: Three cards: the quick start, Bitcoin addresses and the invoice. Read the new locker number for each delivery and the bill. Ask why a fresh address for each payer helps. It keeps payments from being linked to one another.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Alice's first bitcoin, step by step
slides.say: Alice's first bitcoin in four steps: install, address, acquire, confirm. Point at the recovery code note under step one and at the confirmations note. Ask why no account is opened. An address is derived from a key and registered nowhere.
slides.takeaway: Four steps from an empty phone to a first payment

slides.title: An address is a hash with a checksum
slides.say: An address is a hash with a checksum. Point at the four lines: version, payload, checksum, Base58. Ask why a mistyped address is caught, and the answer is the last four bytes check the rest. Students often think the address is the public key; it is a hash of it.
slides.takeaway: A mistyped address is caught by its checksum

slides.title: An invoice is a link with an amount
slides.say: An invoice is a link with an amount. Point at the parsed fields and at the result 15,000 satoshis. Ask what a QR code adds, and the answer is nothing; it is the same text drawn as dots. Students sometimes forget to convert bitcoin to satoshis exactly.
slides.takeaway: A QR code is only this text, drawn as dots

slides.title: Why one address per payer
slides.say: Reusing an address lets anyone link and total your payments. Point at the left column where three payers all use one address and at the right where each payer gets a fresh one. Ask what an onlooker learns in each case. Fresh addresses keep payments apart.
slides.takeaway: A fresh address for each payment keeps payments apart

slides.title: A first payment: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.say: Three cards: receiving bitcoin, getting your first bitcoin and sending and receiving. Read the payment slip, the foreign money and the till. Ask which way suits a student with no bitcoin. Buying from a friend is the simplest.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Four ways to a first bitcoin
slides.say: Four ways to a first bitcoin: buy from a friend, earn it, use an ATM or use an exchange. Read the third column: what each needs from you. Ask which one is simplest, and the answer is a friend. Note that a balance at an exchange is not your keys; recall Mt. Gox.
slides.takeaway: Buying from a friend is simplest; an exchange adds identity checks

slides.title: Sending: coins in, payment and change out
slides.say: A wallet spends whole coins and returns the change. Point at the three coins and at the result 18,500. Ask why the wallet picks 80,000 and not 50,000, and the answer is that 50,000 does not cover 61,500. A common mistake is to think a coin can be cut.
slides.takeaway: You never cut a coin: you spend it and get change

slides.title: Foundations
slides.say: Two old solved problems joined into one system, like two rivers. Read the three beats. Ask which two problems are meant, and the answer is making spam cost work, and agreeing without trust. Students often think Bitcoin solved something nobody had tried.
slides.takeaway: Two old solved problems, joined into one system, like two rivers.

slides.title: Two solved problems, one new system
slides.say: Hashcash from 1997 and the Byzantine generals from 1982 meet in 2008. Point at the two boxes. Ask what each contributes, and the answer is a cost for sending, and agreement without a leader. Neither idea was new; their combination was.
slides.takeaway: Neither idea was new; their combination was

slides.title: From keys to the chain
slides.say: The pipeline the rest of the course walks: keys, addresses, transactions, blocks, mining. Point at the chapter number under each box. Ask which box this chapter has touched already. Each stage trusts only what it can verify.
slides.takeaway: This pipeline is the course syllabus in one row

slides.title: Five cryptographic tools in a wallet
slides.say: Five cryptographic tools in one picture. Point at the two real hashes: one changed character gives an unrelated fingerprint. Ask which tool proves who signed, and the answer is the digital signature. Students often mix up a hash, which has no key, with a keyed hash, which does.
slides.takeaway: Every wallet builds on these five small ideas

slides.title: Computing words under the chapter
slides.say: Everyday computing words under this chapter. Read a row at a time and tie each to where it appeared: explorers in a browser, the node database, a hash of 32 bytes. Ask which term a student is unsure of. Do not skip bits and bytes; later chapters count in them.
slides.takeaway: Plain computing ideas carry Bitcoin

slides.title: How Bitcoin changes without a boss
slides.say: Bitcoin changes without a boss through open proposals. Follow the flow from idea to BIP to reference implementation to each node's decision. Ask who forces an upgrade, and the answer is nobody; each operator chooses. The W3C row shows the same open habit for identity.
slides.takeaway: Anyone may propose; only the nodes that choose to run a change make it real

slides.title: Foundations: key concepts
slides.say: Offchain technology in one card, with Alice, Bob, Carol and Dave in a picture. Read the bar tab comparison. Ask what the chain sees when Alice pays Dave through three channels, and the answer is nothing. Students often think offchain means unsafe.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Two transactions, any number of payments
slides.say: A channel costs two transactions however many payments follow. Point at the result [-1, 8, 98, 998] and at the negative first value. Ask when a channel starts to pay off, and the answer is from the third payment. The first value is negative: one payment alone loses.
slides.takeaway: A channel pays off from the third payment on

slides.title: A channel in three steps
slides.say: A payment channel costs two on-chain transactions however many payments follow. Follow open, update, close. Ask what the Lightning Network adds, and the answer is channels linked so that any peer can pay any other. Offchain also changes what a backup must cover.
slides.takeaway: Two transactions on the chain can carry any number of payments

slides.title: What kind of thing is Bitcoin?
slides.say: Bitcoin's stated characteristics and the architecture behind them. Point at virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust, then at the three structures below. Ask which structure delivers which adjective. Each is engineered, not advertised.
slides.takeaway: Each adjective is engineered, not advertised

slides.title: The chapter in six lines
slides.say: Six lines, one per part. Read each line and point to the slide that proves it. Ask students to say one line in their own words without looking. If a line feels unproven, its code slide carries the receipt.
slides.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, its code slide carries the receipt

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Resources for further reading and watching: the white paper, the book, the developer guides, explorers, the community and the seminal papers. Ask each student to look up block 0 on mempool.space. Every entry is a live link in this file.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.say: Close with the six questions from the start and ask who can now answer each. Give a minute for questions. The aim is that every student can say, in one sentence each, where Bitcoin came from, who holds keys and how a double spend is refused.
slides.takeaway: And where each claim gets its proof
